lines.line: Home tests show what is likely there, not how much or how strong.
lines.note: Anchors: reagents cannot tell how pure or potent drugs are; cannot give dosage information for pressed pills.

lines.line: They can’t tell you if it is one drug or a mix.
A test that looks fine does not prove a drug is safe.
lines.note: Anchors say a negative strip result does not guarantee absence of all synthetic opioids or nitazenes; EUDA attributes the 'false feeling of safety' point to critics.

lines.line: A drug checking service tests in a lab and can tell you more. Colour test kits are the least accurate way to check.
lines.line_fix: A drug checking service that tests in a lab can tell you more. Colour test kits are the least accurate way to check.
lines.note: As written, it says every drug checking service tests in a lab. The EUDA figure lists a range of drug checking technologies, including reagent kits. The anchors support only a lab result being better than a home quick test.

lines.line: Marquis, Mecke or Mandelin colour tests show if a sample reacts like MDMA.
Simon’s test helps tell MDMA from MDA.
Synthetic cathinones are one of the most likely substitutes for MDMA.
Marquis, Simon’s and Froehde colour tests suit amphetamine-type drugs.
Marquis reacts with methamphetamine. Simon’s helps tell it from amphetamine.
The Morris colour test is used to test for cocaine. Marquis is not supposed to react with cocaine.
lines.note: 'Not supposed to' keeps the source's hedge. The same page adds that Marquis has recently sometimes turned light pink-orange with cocaine.

lines.line: The Morris colour test is used to test for ketamine.
Mecke and Liebermann colour tests can tell apart some cathinones.
Ehrlich’s colour test reacts with LSD and drugs like it.
LSD test strips (lysergamide strips) are another test for LSD.
lines.note: The NZ anchor approves lysergamide strips as a stand-alone test for licensed drug checking providers; the line does not claim more than that it is a test for LSD.

lines.line: Ehrlich’s colour test reacts with psilocybin and drugs like it.
lines.note: Same source section warns that Ehrlich's on mushrooms 'can be hit or miss'.

lines.line: It can react even when there is no psilocybin.
lines.note: Source gives the reason: free tryptophan in some non-psychedelic mushrooms can trigger a purple reaction.

lines.line: Ehrlich’s colour test reacts with DMT and drugs like it.
Colour tests give a quick yes-or-no answer about 2C-B.
lines.note: Source describes the colour tests Energy Control runs at venues ('en el propio espacio de ocio'), not home kits specifically; the line makes no stronger claim.

lines.line: No home test tells GHB, GBL and 1,4-BD apart.
lines.note: Source calls 1,4-BD 'BD'.

lines.line: Benzodiazepine test strips give a yes or no for many benzos, but miss some, like etizolam.
Fake pills can look exactly like real ones but contain fentanyl.
lines.line_fix: Fake pills can look exactly like real ones but may contain fentanyl.
lines.note: Anchor says 'may contain fentanyl'. Without 'may', the line can be read as saying fake pills do contain fentanyl.

lines.line: Fentanyl test strips check for fentanyl, but no strip catches every kind.
Fentanyl test strips check for fentanyl, but no strip catches every kind.
Nitazene test strips check for nitazenes, but miss some newer ones.
lines.note: UNODC: desnitazene analogues are often not detected, and the likelihood of missing newer or structurally distinct analogues is rising.

lines.line: Xylazine test strips check for xylazine, but some cutting agents give false results.
lines.note: Source says false positives (from ketamine, levamisole, lidocaine); 'false results' is a fair simplification.

lines.line: Fentanyl test strips check for fentanyl, but no strip catches every kind.
Nitazene test strips check for nitazenes, but miss some newer ones.
lines.note: As heroin#1.

lines.line: Xylazine test strips check for xylazine, but some cutting agents give false results.
lines.note: As heroin#2.

lines.line: Fake pills can look exactly like real ones but contain fentanyl.
lines.line_fix: Fake pills can look exactly like real ones but may contain fentanyl.
lines.note: As benzodiazepines#1: anchor says 'may contain fentanyl'.

lines.line: Fentanyl test strips check for fentanyl, but no strip catches every kind.
Synthetic cannabinoids mixed into cannabis can’t be seen or tasted.
A quick test can be used at home, but it is not as good as a lab check.
The law on test kits differs by state. Many states allow only fentanyl test strips.
lines.note: Source figure is '16 states'; 'many' is a fair rendering. Source dated 26 June 2025.

lines.line: DanceSafe, a non-profit, sells fentanyl test strips and colour test kits online.
lines.line_fix: DanceSafe sells fentanyl test strips and colour test kits online.
lines.note: No anchor says DanceSafe is a non-profit. The pages do say so (footer: 'DanceSafe is a 501(c)3 non-profit registered in the US'), so another option is to add that as an anchor and keep the wording. Anchor #54 (xylazine strip label) supports nothing in this line.

lines.line: New York State posts free fentanyl and xylazine test strips.
lines.note: Campaign launched July 2023; figures as of 1 March 2024. Check the offer is still running.

lines.line: In British Columbia, fentanyl test strips are free at some overdose prevention and health sites.
lines.note: 'Free' rests on Fraser Health #63 ('All drug checking services are free and confidential'). Island Health's 'free' sentence (#59) is only in page metadata.

lines.key: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland#0
lines.line: Colour test kits are legal to buy and own, but may be taken from you at a club or festival door.
lines.note: The 'club or festival door' condition is in the page sentence behind #66/#69 but not in the quote itself; extend the quote.

lines.key: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland#1
lines.line: Some charities and student unions give out free kits.
lines.line_fix: Some charities and student unions give out free kits to students.
lines.note: BDP's free kit is only for University of Bristol students; the Cambridge SU kits are picked up at the SU Lounge or handed out by Colleges. As written, readers may think charities give free kits to anyone. BDP's footer shows 'Reg. Charity Number 291714'; the Cambridge SU page does not mention charity status.

lines.line: Colour test kits are legal to buy and own. NUAA, a charity run by people who use drugs, sells kits online.
lines.note: 'A charity run by people who use drugs' rests only on the anchors' publisher field ('ACNC registered charity and peer-based drug user organisation'). The FAQ page itself does not describe NUAA, so this needs its own anchor if kept.

lines.line: The NZ Drug Foundation posts free fentanyl and nitazene test strips anywhere in New Zealand.
lines.note: Offer is from a post dated 19 December 2024; check it is still running.

lines.line: Colour test kits are legal to buy.
They don’t wake up or don’t answer you.
Their breathing is slow, strange or has stopped.
lines.note: 'Strange' renders ADF's 'abnormal breathing'.

lines.line: They make choking, gurgling or snoring sounds.
Their lips, nails or fingertips turn blue, grey or another odd colour.
The black dots in their eyes are tiny, like pinpoints.
Give naloxone if you have it. It undoes an opioid overdose.
lines.line_fix: Give naloxone if you have it. It can undo an opioid overdose.
lines.note: The flat 'It undoes an opioid overdose' drops WHO's condition ('will reverse ... if administered in time'). FRANK adds that naloxone works 'for only a short period of time'. Naloxone is first aid, so no advice flag.

lines.line: Anyone can give naloxone, including friends and family.
If they are breathing but won’t wake, lay them on their side.
If they are not breathing, start CPR.
Don’t leave them alone, not even for a moment.
Don’t let giving naloxone hold up CPR.
lines.note: FRANK: 'They might still benefit from a naloxone injection, but this mustn't delay starting the required CPR.'

lines.line: Don’t shake them, shout at them or give them coffee.
lines.note: ADF gives this for a very drowsy person (alcohol, heroin or benzodiazepines); FRANK's 'don't shout or shake them' is for a person who is awake.

lines.line: They have chest pain, or pain in the arm, back, neck or jaw.
They have a fit (seizure): shaking or jerking they can’t stop.
They are very hot or sweaty. Hot skin may look red or purple.
lines.note: Simplifies HSE's 'red on white skin or purple on black or brown skin'. Keeping the skin-tone detail would help readers spot flushing on darker skin.

lines.line: Their heart is racing, or beating too slow or unevenly.
If they are passed out but breathing, lay them on their side.
If they are not breathing, start CPR.
If they are awake, talk calmly and tell them the feelings will pass.
lines.line_fix: If they are anxious or panicky, talk calmly and tell them the feelings will pass.
lines.note: ADF says to explain 'the feelings will pass' only to someone who is 'tense, anxious or panicky'. The line ties it to anyone who is awake, including someone with chest pain or overheating. FRANK's 'If they're awake, keep them calm' supports only the calm-talk part.

lines.line: Take them somewhere quiet, away from bright lights, loud music and crowds.
lines.line_fix: If they are agitated or panicky, take them somewhere quiet, away from bright lights, loud music and crowds.
lines.note: Both anchors limit this: ADF to someone 'tense, anxious or panicky', HSE to someone 'agitated and hot', with 'if you can'. Without the condition the line also covers someone who has collapsed, is fitting or has chest pain.

lines.line: Don’t leave them alone, not even for a moment.
Don’t put them in a cold shower or bath.
Don’t give them food or any other drugs.
lines.note: A first-aid 'don't', not combining guidance.

lines.line: They are very hot and can’t cool down.
They have a fit (seizure), or stiff, shaking or twitching muscles.
lines.note: HSE's 'muscle twitches' is listed as a sign of serotonin syndrome.

lines.line: They are very agitated, panicky, paranoid or confused.
They have chest pain, or their heart is racing.
They feel dizzy, have a bad headache or keep being sick.
lines.note: Your Room gives these as signs to 'get help immediately from the medical team' at a festival; healthdirect lists nausea and vomiting among signs of too much MDMA. No anchor names an ambulance for dizziness or headache.

lines.line: At a festival, get the medical team straight away.
If they are too hot, move them somewhere cooler and take off extra clothes.
Let them sip water or a soft drink slowly. Sip, don’t gulp.
lines.note: About water, not a drug, so no advice flag. The sources also give amounts (ADF 'no more than 250ml per hour'; Your Room 500ml/250ml per hour; healthdirect 'about one cup every half hour'), which the line rightly leaves out.

lines.line: If they feel scared or panicky, talk calmly and find somewhere quiet.
Don’t drink lots of water fast. Too much water can kill.
lines.line_fix: Don’t drink lots of water fast. Too much water can be dangerous.
lines.note: No quote says too much water can kill; they say 'dangerous'. The pages do say it: #211's sentence ends '– which can be fatal', and ADF adds 'This can cause coma or death.' Extending quote #211 would let the line stand as written.

lines.line: Don’t leave them alone, not even for a moment.
Don’t put them in a cold shower or bath.
They collapse, stop breathing, or don’t respond to you.
lines.note: ADF's 'collapsed, stopped breathing' sentence comes from its poisonous-mushroom passage. HSE and FRANK cover unresponsiveness for any drug.

lines.line: They have a fit (seizure).
They have chest pain, or their heart is very fast or uneven.
They may be a danger to themselves or others.
lines.note: HSE gives this inside the bullet 'severe distress, confusion or panic - they cannot calm down and may be a danger...'. ADF lists 'increased risk taking' as an ambulance sign.

lines.line: Talk to them in a calm, kind way.
Remind them the effects won’t last. The feelings will pass.
lines.note: Sources give this for a challenging experience or panic, which is the usual crisis for this family.

lines.line: Go with them somewhere calm, away from noise, crowds and bright lights.
lines.line_fix: If they are having a bad trip, go with them somewhere calm, away from noise, crowds and bright lights.
lines.note: All three anchors give this only for distress: HSE 'challenging experience' ('if you can'), ADF 'tense, anxious or panicky', FRANK 'a bad trip'. Without a condition it also covers someone who has collapsed, is fitting or has chest pain.

lines.line: Help them focus on slow, deep breaths.
Poisonous mushroom? Call a poisons centre straight away.
lines.note: The condition and urgency come from the sentence before the quote: 'If you believe you or someone else may have eaten a poisonous mushroom, do not wait for symptoms to occur.' Consider quoting that too.

lines.line: Don’t leave them alone, not even for a moment.
Don’t give them any other drugs.
lines.note: A first-aid 'don't', not combining guidance.

lines.line: If they become violent, don’t put yourself in danger.
lines.note: HSE goes on: 'Move away from the person and call 112 or 999.'

lines.line: They pass out (lose consciousness).
Their breathing is slow, shallow or difficult, or it stops.
They have a fit (seizure).
Their heartbeat is fast, slow or uneven, or they have chest pain.
If they pass out but are breathing, lay them on their side.
If their breathing is weak or has stopped, start CPR.
lines.note: 'Weak' breathing rests only on NIDA, which writes about OTC medicine overdoses (DXM, loperamide). FRANK and HSE say CPR if not breathing.

lines.line: If they are scared or confused, talk calmly and tell them you’ll stay.
Stay with them until help comes, and keep checking their breathing.
Don’t put them in a bath or shower. They could drown.
lines.note: The drowning risk is stated for baths (HSE ketamine); 'shower' comes from HSE's 'do not put the person in a cold shower or bath'.

lines.line: Don’t give them more of the drug, or any other drugs.
lines.note: 'More of the drug' rests on HSE ketamine's 'Avoid taking more ketamine' (comedown advice). A first-aid 'don't', not dosing guidance.

lines.line: Don’t leave them alone, not even for a moment.
They have chest pain, pressure or tightness.
They have a fit (seizure).
They have trouble breathing, or breathe very slowly.
lines.note: ADF says 'slow breathing'. 'Very slowly' sets a higher bar than the source; consider dropping 'very'.

lines.line: They pass out or don’t respond to you.
If they pass out but are breathing, lay them on their side.
If they are not breathing, start CPR.
If they’re anxious or paranoid, talk calmly and remind them it will pass.
Go with them somewhere calm, away from noise, crowds and bright lights.
lines.line_fix: If they are anxious or paranoid, go with them somewhere calm, away from noise, crowds and bright lights.
lines.note: HSE gives this for someone having a challenging experience, adding 'if you can'. Without a condition the line also covers someone who has passed out, is fitting or has chest pain.

lines.line: Don’t leave them alone, not even for a moment.
Don’t give them any other drugs.
lines.note: A first-aid 'don't', not combining guidance.

lines.line: Don’t argue with them or brush off what they feel.
They have passed out and can’t be woken, or don’t respond.
Their breathing is slow, strange or noisy, or it has stopped.
They make choking, gurgling or snoring sounds.
They have a fit (seizure).
Their skin is pale, blue or grey, or cold and clammy.
lines.note: HSE's 'grey' is about lips or fingertips; the line applies it to skin.

lines.line: If they pass out, lay them on their side so they don’t choke.
lines.note: Anchors are alcohol-poisoning pages, but the general FRANK/HSE emergency pages give the same recovery-position advice for any drug.

lines.line: If they’re awake, help them sit up and stay awake.
lines.line_fix: If they’re awake after drinking alcohol, help them sit up and stay awake.
lines.note: Both anchors are alcohol-poisoning advice (NHS 'someone who has drunk too much alcohol'; FRANK's alcohol-poisoning part). The line applies it to all depressants (GHB, benzos). For a very drowsy person who took alcohol, heroin or benzos, ADF instead says to lay them on their side and talk to them.

lines.line: Keep checking their breathing. Be ready to give CPR.
If they are not breathing, start CPR.
Don’t let them drink any more alcohol.
lines.note: Anchors are alcohol-poisoning pages; the line itself names alcohol.

lines.line: Don’t try to make them sick. They could choke.
Don’t leave them alone, not even for a moment.
Someone has swallowed poppers liquid, even with no signs yet.
lines.note: ADF: 'Call an ambulance straight away if you or someone else has swallowed alkyl nitrites – even if no symptoms are present.'

lines.line: They pass out, or don’t respond to you.
They have trouble breathing, or their breathing is slow or not normal.
They have chest pain, or their heartbeat is uneven, slow or stops.
Move lighters and flames away. Make sure there is plenty of fresh air.
If they pass out but are breathing, lay them on their side.
If they are not breathing, start CPR.
Keep calm, reassure them, and speak quietly.
Don’t chase them or hold them down. Effort raises the risk of sudden death.
Don’t let them run or exercise after using.
lines.note: About activity after use, not how much or how to take the drug, so no advice flag.

lines.line: Don’t leave them alone, not even for a moment.
They are in great distress, confusion or panic and can’t calm down.
They may be a danger to themselves or others.
lines.note: HSE gives this inside the severe-distress bullet.

lines.line: They don’t respond, have a fit, or have trouble breathing.
Keep them away from heights, roads and water.
lines.note: 'Heights, roads and water' is in the anchors' heading ('where'), not in either quote; consider quoting the heading. Source is salvia-specific self-care advice.

lines.line: Talk calmly, and remind them the effects won’t last.
If they pass out but are breathing, lay them on their side.
Stay with them until help comes.
Don’t leave them alone, not even for a moment.
Don’t give them any other drugs.
lines.note: A first-aid 'don't', not combining guidance.

lines.line: If they become violent, don’t put yourself in danger.
